en: Compiled by Shi Dunlun from the *Lunben* (Treatise on the Fundamentals), Volume 86, Great Section Three:

Explaining Perception (*saṃjñā*), Mental Formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth. First, the verses list ten sections: 1. Perception and Mental Formations; 2. ... [and so on]. 1. Perception and Mental Formations. 2. ... [and so on].
The characteristics of folly,
the three eyes,
and the four benefits.
Five are the nine knowledges;
six are non-delusion;
seven are the stages of superior progress.
8. The distinctions of the view of self;
9. The three types of conceptualization and practice;
10. The comprehensive category of dharmas, as elaborated extensively in the third [section] of the latter part.
This means that within this section there are three successive repetitions;
therefore, it is said "three.
These three repetitions are not one.
Therefore, it is said "and so forth.
First, in one further section,
the fourfold summary (udāna) of the dharmas is briefly explained.
This is called the "general characteristic of phenomena" (dharmasāmānyalakṣaṇa); it is translated as "seal of the Dharma" (dharmamudrā).
However, upon examining the Sanskrit manuscript, the term "seal of the Dharma" does not appear.
Furthermore, there are two additional sections that extensively clarify the meaning of the first section; therefore,
it is called "Further Extensive."
This is the interpretation and explanation provided by Master Yuan and others.
If one follows the interpretations of Jing, Tai, and others, it is divided into eleven sections;
the tenth section is titled "The Chapter on the General Equality of Dharmas."
The eleventh section is titled "Extensive Explanation of the Three Subsequent [Points].
For now, we shall follow the previous classification;
within the prose commentary, it is divided into ten sections.
The first explains the characteristics of perception and mental formations; the textual structure is clear.
The second explains that foolish persons possess three characteristics.
Furthermore, by means of pride, the characteristics of delusion are distinguished.
Regarding the third [point], the explanation of how the eye of wisdom is far removed from dust and free from defilement is presented in two parts.
Fourth is the explanation of the benefits.
Regarding the terms "correct conventional" (*tathyasaṃvṛti*) and "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*):
according to the *Abhidharma*, that which expresses [the teachings] is called "correct conventional."
The principle that is fully expressed is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Fifth, the explanation of the nine knowledges:
the first five knowledges pertain to the stage prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The latter four knowledges reside in the path of insight into characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-darśana-mārga*).
The knowledge of the flow and turning of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-pravṛtti-jñāna*) arises briefly from three kinds of causes and conditions.
The right knowledge that gathers all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is as follows:
because of the accumulation of suffering, form (*rūpa*) arises;
because of the accumulation of contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*) arises.
Because of the arising of name-and-form, consciousness arises;
thus, through the cessation of the arising of these three,
form, feeling, and consciousness cease.
This is called "reversion and cessation.
Knowledge of the causes of affliction through the object of the relish of craving;
knowledge of the causes of purification through the object of the defects [of that craving].
The wisdom that takes renunciation as its object is pure wisdom.
While in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), by cultivating the first five types of wisdom, one can swiftly realize the latter four.
The sixth is the dwelling of liberation through the absence of delusion.
First, the dwelling free from delusion is explained;
subsequently, the dwelling with delusion is generally revealed. Within this:
First, it is shown that delusion exists and is included within the category of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Next, the different names for the three poisons are explained;
there are fifteen names for greed (*rāga*).
The names for hatred are also fifteen;
the names for delusion are seven.
The distinctions between joy and attachment will be explained later.
Seventh, the explanation of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).
First, the four types of superior progress are clarified;
subsequently, the three types of superior progress-conceptions (*saṃjñā*) are clarified.
Regarding the statement "affliction and harm" up to "cultivating the perception of aversion":
one gives rise to affliction and harm because of separation from friends and relatives and the loss of wealth and possessions.
It is said that herein, from first [discussing] the perception of faults up to finally explaining their causes,
the sequence of cultivation is revealed.
Eighth, the explanation of the distinctions within the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Master Jing said:
"Regarding the statement that 'the three conditions depend upon the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi),' this refers to that which arises within each individual internal body;
that is, one gives rise to the conceptualized view of self by taking one's own body as the object."
Regarding the fourth type of object-condition, which is the view of self based on others— that is, the conceptualization arising with respect to another’s body—
one does not conceive of that body as one's own self;
rather, one merely conceptualizes the other’s body, thinking of such a self as being "good" or "bad," and so forth.
The passage from "I see [the self] as the basis for the arising of the conceit 'I am'" up to "just as on a pure and perfect face" is a metaphor for the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*).
"The substance and image serve as the basis for the production of a reflected image" refers to the following.
Regarding the self-conceived "self" as the basis for the image, and further distinguishing others based on that self-conceived self—
this is called the "image. It is that which,
depending upon its own basis, gives rise to inferior, middling, or superior perceptions.
Furthermore, based on what others conceive as a self, one compares it with one's own self and gives rise to notions of inferiority or superiority.
The intermediate analogy states:
"In this way, due to false discrimination, one takes the view of a self that relies upon its own basis as a condition."
The arising of the view of self based on others as its support is like the example given regarding the underlying substance (*upādāna*).
One should know that for those who give rise to the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*) based on the co-emergent view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the illustration differs from the previous one.
Pride that arises from the conceptual view of self (parikalpita-ātmadṛṣṭi) and leads to disparaging others is [pride];
pride that arises from the innate view of self (sahaja-ātmadṛṣṭi) and leads to one’s own exaltation is merely termed *mada* (intoxication/arrogance).
Thus, there is a distinction.
For example, when a person with clear vision looks into a vessel of pure water and observes their own eyes and ears— the remaining details of which should be understood as previously described—
this serves as a metaphor for the arising of pride from the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
From this "view of a self-identity in all its aspects" up to the one "of great beneficence":
it is praised that the Buddha’s teaching possesses the superior capacity to extinguish the view of a self-identity.
Both the Buddha and his disciples are called "of great beneficence" because they instruct practitioners.
"Exclusively by means of this single causal condition, until it is fully satisfied"—
this refers to what is called "repaying kindness according to one's capacity" through the practice of the teachings as explained.
Master Tai said:
Because a mirror is produced by human effort, it is used as a metaphor for discriminative perception;
because water is not produced by human effort, it is used as a metaphor for innate perception.
The ninth [section] explains these three types of characteristics.
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have ceased,
it is called the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
The first refers to past karma.
First, it refers to the eternal cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have arisen in the past and the present.
Second, it refers to the eternal cessation of conditioned phenomena that, having already arisen,
perish according to their own nature and do not abide ultimately.
Third, because one is forever liberated from all afflictions,
they are abandoned without remainder and will not arise again hereafter.
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are extinguished through these three perceptions, it is called "quiescence" (*śānti*).
This is not like the absolute non-existence of a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns.
[This point is] explained extensively later in the third section of the tenth chapter, the "General Exposition of the Dharma."
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the analysis of the four dharma-uddānas;
second, a detailed explanation of their meaning through two successive sequences.
Regarding the middle [section], Master Jing said:
"The statement that 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent' is the seal of the conditioned dharmas."
"All conditioned phenomena are suffering" is the seal of the dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*).
This is the summary verse (*udāna*) for the first gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), which establishes impermanence as the first and suffering as the second.
"All phenomena are without self" is established as the third seal of all phenomena based on the liberation of emptiness.
"Nirvāṇa is tranquil" is established as the fourth summary of the Dharma (dharmoddāna), the seal of the Dharma of nirvāṇa, based on the gateway of signlessness.
Master Tai said:
"Uddāna has two pronunciations.
If pronounced with a heavy tone, it means 'to gather up things and bestow them as gifts upon others.'"
If one speaks in a low voice, saying "this" or "the summarized meaning," such as "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" and so forth,
this is the summarized meaning of all dharmas.
Therefore, following this brief statement,
two further sequences are now raised to provide a detailed explanation.
Within these:
The first sequence clarifies the mind that is to be remedied, eliminated, and turned back;
the latter sequence then clarifies the practice that serves as the remedy.
Within the former:
Regarding the statement "desire accompanied by resolute conviction," it means that through four types of *udāna* (summaries), one generates a longing for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Through the four types of *udāna* which teach the four seals of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*), one desires to abandon impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and so forth within all conditioned phenomena.
One desires to cultivate the practice of the signless path that leads to the tranquility of nirvāṇa;
furthermore, regarding those who develop a desire for the tranquility of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) until their minds turn back [from worldly involvement], and so forth.
First, by citing his lack of delight, it can be understood that his desire for it [is absent].
As for the statement, "Furthermore, due to two conditions,
mindfulness is lost," this means that because of these two conditions, one becomes terrified of selflessness and retreats from it.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, as for this patience and aspiration, because his mind is still dull and so forth":
because he has not yet become habituated to this patience regarding selflessness,
although he understands that there are only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), his mind remains dull with respect to selflessness.
"Carrying me [to liberation], he causes me to understand through repeated reflection until my mind turns back.
The following clarifies the practice that serves as the remedy.
It says: "In the presence of wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life (sabrahmacārin), one reveals [the truth] exactly as it is."
When contemplating selflessness, one observes that the mind becomes obstructed.

Speaking with truthful words, one should not act with arrogance or deceit by concealing what one understands; rather, one should say, "Because of that thorough knowledge," up to "and the fruit thereby attained."
This refers to the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which, based on three things, conceives of a self; it is thoroughly known by right knowledge.
The seeds of this view of a self are called latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Because of the conception of a self, one consequently conceives of [the self] as either annihilated or eternal.
Therefore, it is said that the view of self is the basis for the two views of annihilationism and eternalism;
from this, the attachment and latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the two views of self and body arise,
which are termed the "fruits obtained."
Within the seven stages of skillful means (*saptavidha-upāya*) that accord with contemplation, right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) is able to comprehend this matter.
Below, it sets forth the three objects (*ālambana*) conditioned by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*):
first, the grasped (*grāhya*), which refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
The second, the grasper, refers to the four types of grasping (*upādāna*).
The third, the manner of such grasping, refers to the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
The methods of grasping should be understood according to their respective order as previously explained.
Regarding "being the locus of dependence for the mind of dual grasping":

one interpretation holds that the four stations of consciousness (*catasraḥ vijñānasthitayaḥ*) serve as the locus of dependence for the two minds previously mentioned— the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
Second interpretation:
The three things serve as the basis for the two types of mind—those of "I" and "mine"—mentioned previously.
Furthermore, based on these three things, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) may arise.
It serves as the basis for the two views of annihilationism and eternalism;

therefore, in the preceding general discussion, the explanation of self-clinging with respect to the three objects already clarifies that it is the basis for both the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
It should be understood that, according to their sequence as previously stated, these constitute the objective bases for the mind of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
Furthermore, regarding "all the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) present therein, up to and including their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)," etc.:
This explains thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) by way of the fruit obtained.
Furthermore, regarding the statement: "If, when the right view that should be applied to what is to be thoroughly known is active, how much more so will one attain liberation? [it means as follows].
This is the wholesome state conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
If it accords with clear realization (*abhisamaya*) and reaches the point of being capable of renunciation,
it is the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
If one has already initiated [the process] such that liberation is attained only upon reaching [a certain stage],
this refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth.
It should be understood that when these three views operate, there is this distinction.
The right view of the stage conducive to liberation;
the right view of the stage of penetration;
and the right view of clear realization.
The distinctions among the three views are as previously explained.
In the fourth major section, the explanation of "swift penetration" (*kṣiprābhijñā*) and so forth,
ten categories are first set forth in verse.
First, swift penetration;
second, the essential nature;
third, the objective sphere of knowledge.
Fourth, the flow of transmigration;
fifth, the practice of contentment;
sixth, the conformity with the stream.
Seventh, the characteristics of what is to be known and abandoned;
eighth, conceptualization;
ninth, establishing the discordant provisions.
In the extensive prose commentary following the "Chapter on the Equality of the Deeds of the Ten Teachers," there are ten sections.
Regarding the initial explanation of swift penetration:
first, the three dharmas are clarified;
subsequently, the five kinds of gradual stages are clarified.
In the first section, the three powers are distinguished so that one may attain swift supernatural penetration;
next, the distinctions between knowledge and vision are clarified;
and finally, the cultivation of the four types of skillfulness is explained.
To begin with,
regarding the power of repeated practice (*abhyāsa-bala*):
it consists of constant performance and constant turning.
One should never set a limit for oneself, thinking, "I shall attain the exhaustion of outflows on this very day, tomorrow, or the day after.
By not setting such a limit, one will not become weary.
Within the distinctions between knowledge (*jñāna*) and vision (*darśana*), there are nine pairs.
Furthermore, there is that which is both form (*rūpa*) and object of cognition (*vijñeya*);
this was formerly called "the mother of knowledge" (*jñānamātṛ*).
Master Jing says that according to the Tripiṭaka master,
these are still objects of cognition; thus,
there is the material object of cognition and the reflected image of the material object of cognition.
The Master Da says:
This refers to "the objective realm" (viṣaya).
Below, the four types of skillfulness are explained.
The text has three parts:
first, the analysis of skillful means;
second, the analysis of the support and the supported.
Next, the path of purification is explained.
Regarding the first [of its two parts]:
it is said that one thoroughly knows all objects as they truly are.
The objective domain of the four foundations of mindfulness consists of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
Regarding the emergence from meditative states: this refers to the emergence from the root of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) upon exiting the first dhyāna.
This continues up until the emergence of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) from the fourth dhyāna.
Next, regarding the analysis of that which serves as the basis,
Master Jing says:
It should be understood that for one who thus diligently cultivates skillful means, there are four kinds of bases (*āśraya*).
Regarding the "basis and that which is based" (*āśrita*), it is explained generally that all four [preceding categories] possess both a basis and that which is based upon it.
The meaning of the "basis" refers to the practice of contemplation and the correct application of effort;
it is the meaning of being the basis for the aforementioned four types of skillfulness.
The meaning of the "based upon" is as follows:
This means that because the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*) depend upon diligence (*vīrya*), they are the supported;
the remaining ignorance (*avidyā*) remains until purity is attained.
Master Tai says:
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment previously distinguished are collectively categorized into four types of skillful activities (*kauśalya-vastu*).

The first two consist of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). The first three—the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), etc.—constitute the basis for reliance (*niśraya-vastu*), as they pertain to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Subsequently, the various untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas possessed by those in training (*śaikṣa*), such as the power of the single faculty and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), serve as the basis for support.
The following clarifies the path of purification through two successive explanations.
As previously stated:
"Those dharmas become pure only after [the purification] through the path of purity" refers to the seven preceding categories of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
This refers to the subsequent purification following the attainment of the pure path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The subsequent explanation of the five kinds of gradual stages can be understood according to the text.
The second [section] explains its own nature.
First, a general indication;
second, a detailed explanation of the five phrases.
First, "the lifespan is limited" and so forth:
this illustrates that while one may freely grasp or discard lumps of clay,
the body destined for death cannot be extended by even a single moment as one might wish.
Second, because it is produced by causes;
third, because it is subject to wear and destruction;
fourth, because it is so taught by the Noble Ones.
Fifth, because the enjoyment of desires is fulfilled.
Regarding the statement that "three kinds of causes and conditions can bring about fulfillment," Master Jing says:
Generosity is the cause of material wealth,
or it is the cause for the perfection of one's own being;
it is the fruit obtained through the training of the sense faculties and the cultivation of loving-kindness within the desire realm.

This is the fruit obtained through the practice of taming the faculties of vast and sublime sentient beings and through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
it is the cause for the perfection of making offerings to vast and sublime sentient beings.
One interpretation states: first, because practicing generosity, ethical discipline, and the subduing of the six sense faculties together, one’s material resources are perfected;
second, because it is the fruit obtained through the cultivation of loving-kindness within the desire realm, one’s physical body is perfected.
Third, because one takes loving-kindness as the primary cause and does not harm sentient beings, one attains the perfection of the third [stage].
The third is the sphere of liberating wisdom (*mukti-jñāna*).
First, the practice of wisdom is distinguished.
In the subsequent analysis of the cessation of delusion within the preceding section,
the phrase "knowledge of what has been attained and what has not yet been attained" refers to knowledge previously acquired and knowledge never before acquired.
To say that "this state does not exist" is the knowledge of its non-existence;
it is the wisdom that realizes the non-existence of what is conceptually imputed (*parikalpita*).
To say that "in this state, there is something else which is known as non-empty" is the wisdom of non-emptiness.
Because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not empty, it is known as the wisdom of non-emptiness.
The following clarifies the practice for severing ignorance.
Master Jing said:
Among these, only eight types are mentioned.
The first three are general studies of all phenomena.
First, that which is produced from the water element.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "form-phenomena (*rūpadharma*) mostly arise from water," and that "the two kinds of selflessness appear as if they were a self," these refer collectively to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Regarding "the third, because one is unable to act according to one's will":
once born, one perishes and cannot act according to one's desires. The latter five [characteristics] are categorized according to the aggregates (*skandha*).
Form is like a mass of foam.
Because it arises from the conjunction of the three [elements] and resembles them, there is foam when these three factors—clouds, earth, and rain—are present.
Thus, the aggregate of form is now produced by a multitude of conditions.
Feeling is like a floating bubble.
That which manifests the known object is a metaphor for pleasant feeling;
that which burns is painful feeling.
That which is capable of causing delusion and confusion is the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Furthermore, these three meanings may collectively serve as metaphors for the three types of sensation.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is like a mirage.
Regarding "because the root of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) has been severed":
perception (saṃjñā) is the root of views;
by contemplating and transcending perception, one eliminates the root of the view of a self-identity.
Regarding "due to the differentiation of the causes of the various types of self-entities":
the mirage arises from many causes;
it can be known that the moments produced by the causes of men, women, and the multitudes do not remain still.
The formations are like the trunk of a plantain tree.
When consciousness that possesses grasping arises based on the four stations of consciousness, it initiates various types of self-entities and corresponding phenomena that follow along with them.
This outflowing consciousness, depending upon the four stations of consciousness, performs actions such as demerit and merit; its intrinsic nature is unreal.
Like the trunk of a plantain tree,
when the eight consciousnesses arise and cease, their essence is not real;
they are like illusory phenomena.
These eight have been briefly explained;
the explanations for the remaining seven characteristics are as found in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
Some explain that herein each of the five aggregates is to be contemplated through three meanings.
Thus, there are fifteen characteristics.
Regarding the three aspects of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*): first, form is produced by water.
Second, because the two kinds of selflessness appear as the grasping at signs of a self;
third, because they are not capable of being manipulated according to one's will. It is by virtue of possessing these three meanings [that they are so designated].
Regarding the understanding that form is like foam and the three aspects of the aggregate of sensation:
they arise from the conjunction of the three— sense faculty, object, and consciousness.
Second, because it is like rain falling from clouds onto the earth through their threefold conjunction;
third, because bubbles arise upon it.
Thus, one should realize that feeling is like a bubble.
Regarding the three aspects of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): first, it is like a mirage;
second, it is capable of illuminating, like fire which is capable of burning.
Third, because they share the characteristic of being able to delude sentient beings. Regarding the three aspects of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*):
first, severing the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) like cutting a plantain tree.
Second, it is proven that the various categories of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) arise from causes with distinct differences, such that not a single real essence can be found.
Third, because there is no similar phenomenon that remains even for a moment after the measure of a single instant (*kṣaṇa*).
The three aspects of the aggregate of consciousness are:
first, contaminated consciousness;
second, consciousness that relies upon the four stations of consciousness.
Third, because it functions as the various cognitions that transform and evolve all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Fourth is the explanation of the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*).
This section consists of three parts.
First, the two worlds are raised to distinguish their differences;
next, the fivefold circulation of birth and death is distinguished;
finally, it is clarified that this circulation is bound by five characteristics.
At the beginning and end [of a kalpa], the receptacle world is separated from its prior and subsequent limits by twenty empty kalpas;
this is called the "severance of the prior and subsequent limits."
Furthermore, regarding the permanent severance of the causes of the vessel-like world and of birth and death, this refers only to that which is sustained by common conceptualization;
thus it is said that the principle of non-interruption applies.
However, the causes for one's own body and the external vessel-world are likewise severed.
Furthermore, while the vessel-like cycle of birth and death (bhājanasaṃsāra) ceases and then recurs—
just as the eon of emptiness (śūnyakalpa) undergoes a single period of interruption before resuming—
the cycle of birth and death pertaining to the category of sentient beings (nikāyasaṃsāra) is severed by the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and never continues again.
Next, the five characteristics of transmigration are distinguished as in the text.
Below, it is explained that which is bound by these five characteristics.
What is meant by "that which is truly capable of binding" refers to its own kind [of afflictions],
such as the lack of weariness toward suffering and so forth.
The practitioner does not grow weary of their own aggregate of suffering;
for this aggregate of suffering is precisely that which binds.
This is the fifth [section], the practice of contentment.
First, the matter of contentment is distinguished;
subsequently, the path of craving is elucidated.
Within the former [section]:
Human beings have many worldly activities,
like those rushing toward sensual desires;
the gods of the Heaven of Cessation from Activity rest from such activities.
Standing is like the meditative stage of the Brahma-heaven;
sitting is likewise.
The Peak of Existence is tranquil,
like lying down;
below, it clarifies the path of craving.
The text is divided into three parts.
First, it clarifies the path of the five elements (*pañca-dhātu*).
Second, it clarifies the path of craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*).
The latter clarifies the characteristics of the causes and fruits of the two types of paths of wandering in craving.
Regarding the first, it says:
"It should be known that therein, according to their respective order, there are distinctions such as 'treading' and so forth."
The first and second are called "striding";
the third is called "standing";
and the fourth is called "sitting."
The last one is called "lying down.
Next, regarding the four paths of craving,
first the four paths are explained.
This belongs to the four subsequent lines.
Within the preceding section,
regarding the phrase "whether transforming or practicing within that which has been attained," etc.:
That is to say, regarding the requisites one has obtained, according to one's desire, whether one sells them to others or uses them oneself,
one feels attachment toward these objects as well as toward all forms of existence.
Because it initiates karma,
it is connected to the following four lines.
One should know that the four paths proceed accordingly, such as "tending toward" (toward birth) and so forth.
As it is said, the four stations such as "tending toward" (*pragbhāra*) and so forth,
which are mentioned in relation to others, likewise belong to the four paths in their respective order.
The following clarifies the characteristics of the causes and fruits of the two types of paths of wandering in craving.
First, the distinctions among the characteristics of the fruits are analyzed.
Regarding the phrase "the various and all-encompassing distinctions of bodies":
The five destinies (*gati*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are called "various," while the single destiny within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is called "one kind.
This subsequently clarifies that because there is a distinction in causes, there is now a distinction in results.
Regarding the phrase "this very distinction," it refers to the body as it is encompassed by five types of conduct;
as for its various distinctions:
There are two interpretations of this:
one says it refers to the five types of formations, such as "future existence" (punarbhava) and so forth;
another says it refers to the body comprised of the five aggregates, such as form (rūpa) and so forth.
Now, according to the subsequent explanation below, the latter interpretation is superior.
Regarding the sixth explanation, which concerns "flowing with the current" (anuloma), we shall first distinguish what it means to flow with the current.
The latter part generally clarifies the reversal of the stream. Within the former [section], it asks:
"What is meant by being drifted and submerged? It refers to the phenomena of saṃsāra and so forth among all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), according to their respective sequences," and so on.
There is an interpretation which states: regarding the five types of processes of transmigration previously explained— namely, that place and so forth—

It is called "quiescence" because the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of vision have been exhausted.
Up to the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation on the level of the sphere of nothingness,
it is therefore called "cool"; this is because the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation on the level of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have been exhausted.
It is called "dignified silence" (*pratisaṃlayana*).
One interpretation holds that it is "tranquil" because the fetters of all afflictions have been severed.
It is called "purity" because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have been abandoned;
it is called "tranquility" because the maturation (*vipāka*) has been abandoned.
Furthermore, due to three conditions, consciousness proceeds and abides in consciousness, yet all such states are non-existent.
First, because its own substance is not defiled;
second, because it is not defiled by anything else;
and third, because it lacks the accompaniment of other defiled consciousnesses.
The meaning of this can be understood.
This concludes the sixth major section:
the explanation of the factors of abandonment (*prahāṇa-aṅga*) and so forth.
The preceding verse lists seven categories:
first, the factors of abandonment;
second, the actual manifestation.
Third, the objective condition of the three types of conduct; fourth, the incomparable teaching;
fifth, the fourfold assembly of sentient beings.
Six destinies have four [stages],
and the seventh has five ultimate [stages].
Next, in the prose explanation:
There are seven further sections.
First, the explanation of the branches of abandonment:
the fruit attained is termed "abandonment."
The causes that are capable of manifesting [the truth] are called "limbs" (*aṅga*).
Regarding the second explanation, there are twelve ways of manifesting clarity.
Master Jing said:
It is revealed as it truly is:
first, there is hearing each individually;
second, there is the grasping of good and evil.
The correct teaching is one;
direct and inferential cognition are two;
and the particular and the universal are two.
The nature of things as they are (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*) and the nature of things in their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) constitute two.
Entering the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) and reaching the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*) constitute two.
Thus says the Master.
As for the statement "twelve," it refers to the correct apprehension of the [four] truths and so forth;
however, they are not complete.
There is a master’s interpretation:
first, listening;
second, goodness.
Third, false apprehension;
fourth, the authority of correct teaching;
fifth, the object of direct perception.
Sixth, the object of inference;
seventh, the specific characteristic;
eighth, the general characteristic.
Ninth, as-it-is-ness;
tenth, exhaustiveness;
eleventh, entry into the stage of seeing.
The twelfth stage is the ultimate stage of the twelve bases (*āyatana*). This third section, on the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*),
first provides a general outline.
Next is the specific explanation, followed by the general conclusion.
Within the specific explanation:
There are four types of persons:
first, ordinary beings within the Dharma;
second, householders who are ordinary beings.
Third, non-Buddhist ordinary beings;
fourth, those in training within the internal Dharma.
Among these four types of persons:
Each has two phrases:
first, explaining that which is not as it truly is;
second, explaining that which is as it truly is.
Master Tai said:
"This is called 'manifesting as it truly is' because it brings about purification within those four who do not know things as they truly are."
The fourth section explains the peerless teaching.
First, it distinguishes the peerlessness of the teaching;
subsequently, it clarifies the distinctions of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Fifth, the explanation of the four classes of sentient beings.
Master Jing’s commentary states:
"First, those born in the heavens through karma who exclusively practice indulgence; these are precisely the Māras and Brahmās mentioned previously."
Second, there is the transformation through a one-sided cause,
which refers to the longing for those qualities such as being a śramaṇa and so forth.
Third, those sentient beings who delight in nirvāṇa;
fourth, various types of beings,
namely, those who are attached to and enjoy the fruits [of their actions].
Thus, the first person is one who delights in grasping at the fruits of future craving;
the second is one who practices the cause in order to seek that aforementioned fruit.
Or, at times, there are those who possess the provisions for nirvāṇa and are free from all negligence;
this is the third type of person.
Among the three aforementioned groups of sentient beings, one should understand that they correspond to the worldly extremes of origination and cessation.
Regarding the distinction between these two assemblies,
it should be stated: "One should know that the limit of the cessation of the world" clarifies that the initial Māras and Brahmās who receive worldly fruits are subject to the common law of cessation.
One should know that regarding the limit of the origination and cessation of those [aggregates],
this second category of conditioned formations seeking the cause of heaven is a phenomenon subject to the cessation of its own origination;
and as for the *satkāya* (the view of a self-identity), it likewise pertains to the limit of the origination and cessation of its own origination.
This is the third type of person who delights in nirvāṇa and is free from all negligence;
their entire causal process is likewise the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*). *Sakkāya* refers to the body.
This is the Truth of Suffering,
characterized by impermanence and cessation.
That which brings about its cessation is the abandonment of negligence.
This is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*). Because it is a phenomenon that can be abandoned and extinguished,
it is called the limit of the extinction of that origination.
Regarding the phrase "among that fourth group of sentient beings," this refers to the fourth type, the mixed class of persons.
It should be understood that the term *satkāya* [refers to this].
This is suffering;
that is its origination. This is origination.
That which is cessation refers to the path leading to cessation;
this is the Truth of the Path.
Regarding "differentiation":
because there are four distinct truths,
it is called differentiation.
Master Tai says:
"As for 'reaching the satkāya,' this further clarifies the mundane world."
Since *satkāya* is a synonym for the world,
the limits of its origination and cessation are explained again in their respective order as the limits of the origination and cessation of that [world].
The Master Da said:
"Among these four statements,
the first three specifically clarify the three types of persons."
The fourth phrase collectively clarifies that the three preceding types of persons constitute the fourth person.
Regarding the term "śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas," this refers to non-Buddhist śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who seek the retribution of rebirth in heaven.
The phrase "one should know" is an exhortation;
this passage may be said to mean "it should be known."
This is because it encourages the cessation of suffering and so forth.
Regarding the sixth [member], the Path, there are four [aspects].
As for the statement that three depend on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and one depends on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*):
Master Jing said:
"The Path of Seeing consists of the first three truths;
the Path of Cultivation consists of the Truth of the Path."
Because within the path of cultivation one is able to abandon the remaining origination, realize cessation,
and cultivate the remaining paths that exhaust the outflows,
it receives the name "path of cultivation" (bhāvanāmārga).
The Master Da said:
"This passage is an exposition of a single aspect;
it does not exhaust the full principle."
This is because the three meanings of knowledge (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) can all be found within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Fifth, the seventh [topic] is the explanation of the ultimate (*niṣṭhā*):
first, it refers to having realized suffering and its cause such that they are exhausted without remainder.
Second, it is capable of accomplishing the welfare of others, as all one's own welfare is fully perfected;
third, because it attains ultimate abandonment and knowledge;
fourth, because it is able to reach the city of final nirvāṇa.
Because, having already entered [the first dhyāna], one is able to abide securely in that noble dwelling (*āryavihāra*),
the text contains no numerical indicators such as "one" or "two," but merely the word "because" (*hi*) to which one must seek a connection.
Next, regarding the statement that within the first characteristic there are four types of distinctions—such as severing affection—and so forth, which should be understood as previously explained:
this refers to the aforementioned matter of relinquishing one's parents and others.
Because there is no debt in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and because there is no further existence (*punarbhava*) in the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*),
it is said that there is no further existence and no rebirth.
This refers to the initial realization that suffering and its causes have been exhausted without remainder.
Regarding the second characteristic, one should understand as previously explained all the distinctions such as "an arhat who has exhausted all outflows" and so forth.
This refers to the realization of arhatship as previously described— the liberation from all outflows—
and furthermore, being endowed with four meanings is termed the characteristic of an arhat.
First, the meaning that one’s own task is already perfected and one should perform the tasks of others.
Second, because it is the principle of the universal pervasion of all that should be attained for one's own benefit;
third, because it is the principle of realizing the dwelling in happiness in the present life through the permanent cessation of the causes of future formations.
This is because it corresponds to the meaning of transcending the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*) and entering the stage of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*).
This refers to the aforementioned passage: "capable of serving as the welfare of others, the fulfillment of one's own welfare," and so forth.
Regarding the third characteristic, it states: "because all activities that are ultimately final have been completely severed."

"Exhausting karma" means that all karmic actions have been brought to an end. "Because there is ultimate stainlessness and all afflictions are completely severed" means that the afflictions have been exhausted.
These two constitute abandonment;
this is what was previously referred to as "attaining ultimate abandonment" and "possessing ultimate holy life."
To cultivate the path exhaustively is what was previously referred to as "attaining wisdom," which,
regarding the fourth characteristic, is like the worldly [analogy] of possessing five kinds of characteristics.
This provides an analogy to illustrate the Dharma.
Master Tai said:
"To have no expectations regarding others."
Therefore, it is not something desired by oneself or others.
Since Māra has been subdued,
it is said that "the banner has fallen."
The explanation of the fifth characteristic can be understood by following the text.
The seventh major section explains the two chapters and so forth.
The preceding verse enumerates eleven sections.
The first two chapters are general summaries;
the subsequent three, which contain variations, constitute three sections, making four in total.
Five: resolute conviction;
six: abandonment;
seven: transmigration.
8. Those who possess existence;
9. Those who are impure and those who are pure; 10.
Teachers of what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken.
The term "and so forth" includes the eleventh section.
Next, it is explained in prose within the commentary.
There are further eleven sections.
The first explains the general summary of the two chapters.
This summary briefly subsumes all categories of the dark side (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) and the white side (*śuklapakṣa*) by means of three points.
Regarding the first point, "by way of the phenomena to be fully known," this clarifies that one attains nine bases of full knowledge (*parijñā-sthāna*),
which comprise all contaminated (*sāsrava*) suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
Second, "by way of thorough knowledge" refers precisely to the nine types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) which constitute the essence of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Third, "by way of accomplishing thorough knowledge" refers to...
Thus, the Noble Path, as well as the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Noble Disciples,
are all conditions for the attainment of complete knowledge (*parijñā*).
Both Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*) belong to the category of the "white" side (*śuklapakṣa*).
Since the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) collectively subsume the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*),
it is said to be "a portion of the white category" (*śuklapakṣa*).
From here on, the following explains the dharmas that cannot be defined (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the statement that even up until after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa it remains undeclared:
among the ninety-six paths, all claim their own original teacher to be a Tathāgata who possesses the ten titles.
Accordingly, when asked whether the Tathāgata exists or does not exist after his parinirvāṇa, they maintain that both [possibilities] cannot be spoken of.
The following explains the reason.
To begin with, according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), even that [Tathāgata] is unfindable; how much more so could his cessation or his path be either existent or non-existent?
Within the ultimate truth, the Tathāgata, who is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti-nāman*), is fundamentally unfindable.
How much more so after their cessation can one speak of existence or non-existence?

Thus the treatise says: "In the ultimate truth, conditioned phenomena are empty like illusions because they arise dependently; unconditioned phenomena do not exist as realities because they do not arise, resembling flowers in the sky."
Regarding the statement, "If one relies on conventional truth, how could there be existence, non-existence, and so forth?": If,
within the context of the conventional path, one establishes the Tathāgata based upon conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), then after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
the substance of those formations would necessarily cease to exist.
If one asks where the Tathāgata is conventionally established,
and since the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist as an object of discourse,
it would be unreasonable to posit his existence even in the context of nirvāṇa, and so forth.
Nirvāṇa is manifested through non-activity and cannot be said to exist;
how, then, could one establish the Tathāgata on the basis of it?
Furthermore, one should not posit that it does not exist, lest one should disparage the established nature of the wondrously existent Nirvāṇa.
Since it cannot be said that it exists, nor can it be said that it does not exist,
one proceeds by means of conventional designation to establish the Tathāgata as having a nature that is both existent and non-existent.
Furthermore, from this point on, regarding this nirvāṇa...
To distinguish the various names for nirvāṇa:
since nirvāṇa is precisely realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
why is it said that it is not an object of direct perception?
The commentary explains:

This refers precisely to that which is cognized by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of non-conceptual meditative concentration (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*); it is now distinguished from what is obtained through the direct perception of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) in a distracted state of mind.
Therefore, it is said to be "not cognized by direct perception."
The second [point] explains the difference between the internal and external modes of bearing burdens.

Regarding the internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*), that which bears the burden and that which is borne are both, by way of their essential nature, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*); thus, they are distinguished as subject and object.
As for those who possess virtues within:
This refers to "that which is borne" and so forth.
Alternatively, the three phrases beginning with "constantly bearing" may also be termed the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Regarding the third [point], there is a distinction between internal and external fetters.
Regarding the statement, "The external bonds are easy to understand; as for the causes and conditions of bondage, the means of liberation, and the expedient methods for liberation," Master Jing said:
"Because the causes and conditions of external bondage are not of only one kind."
It is said again and again: "Bound, bound.
Even the attainment of liberation is not of a single form.
It is said again and again: "Released, released."
There is another explanation:
external bondage is easy to understand, as are the causes and conditions of bondage;
likewise, liberation and the causes and conditions of liberation [are easy to understand].
Internally, it is difficult to comprehend how all things are bound together.
The fourth [section] explains the commonality and difference between the Buddha and the Arhat;
this is precisely where the third [section] differs.
The Tathāgata and the arhat liberated through wisdom (prajñāvimukta) are identical in one respect by virtue of sharing the same name,
namely "liberated" (vimukta).
However, they are said to be distinct in three respects.
First, manifest perfect enlightenment;
second, being able to teach the Dharma;
third, practicing the correct conduct.
The preceding section consists of four parts.
First, herein the Tathāgata spontaneously cultivated the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and attained manifest, perfect awakening.
Second, having attained manifest, perfect awakening, he fully realized all phenomena.
3. Having thus realized the supreme Dharma, the following clarifies the liberation from the two obstacles.
4. He serves as the peerless and unique teacher of liberation for the assembly of devas.
To fully comprehend these four characteristics is called spontaneous, equal-enlightened bodhi;
it is not shared with the śrāvakas.
Furthermore, from the section beginning with "the meaning of dependence on others" (*paratantra-artha*) onwards,
it clarifies that there are five characteristics of the unique nature of the speaker,
as stated in the text.
There are three aspects to the unique practice of the Threefold Knowledge (trividyā).
First, the śrāvaka first relies upon the Tathāgata and subsequently practices the correct conduct;
the Tathāgata, however, has no reliance whatsoever.
First, each acts according to their own spiritual lineage (*gotra*) in their correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*).
Third, there is a distinction between the two practices being obtainable or unobtainable:

in the bodies of *śrāvakas*, only the attainment or non-attainment [of these practices] exists, whereas in the bodies of Bodhisattvas who are not in their final existence, both practices are obtainable.
That is to say, the accomplishment and non-accomplishment constitute one [category].
Furthermore, manifesting a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) as being on the verge of attaining perfect awakening and the final existence-body (antyabhavika-kāya) constitute two.
If one has already accomplished it, they will become a teacher of the Great Master’s teaching in this present life.
This means that I cause all beings to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and bring them to final liberation.
Because it brings benefit in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*), it manifests the functional power of the explicit teaching (*nītārtha*).
Therefore, it is said to "fulfill the Great Teacher’s teaching."
Furthermore, those who have already achieved this are capable of being entrusted with the Master’s treasury of the Dharma;
therefore, it is said that they "fulfill the Master’s teaching.
Fifth is the explanation of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
The sixth [section] explains the two types of abandonment;
the seventh explains the process of transmigration.
Both may be understood according to the text.
The eighth [section] explains the existence of natures.
First, the three natures of existence are distinguished as that which is to be eliminated;
subsequently, the three abandonments are distinguished as the remedies.
This refers to one who is without attachment; that is,
with the exception of the nature of the initial existence,
they do not take delight in it.

The abandonment of the first two [realms] and the detachment from cessation and so forth constitute the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*), the realm of dispassion (*virāgadhātu*), and the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
Excluding the third,
the ninth explains non-virtuous impurity.
Non-virtuous impurity.

That is to say, prior to the path of seeing, one employs the contaminated contemplation of emptiness and non-self to suppress the notions of "I" and "mine," as well as the four bonds and the three objects of possession.
The three types of possession (*parigraha*) and the four fetters (*saṃyojana*) are as stated in the text.
The four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) perform the practice of the non-self (*anātman*).
Therefore, it is said to be comprised within the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*). It should be understood that it is not thoroughly purified due to two causes and conditions:
first, the practice of the contemplations on emptiness and non-self arises intermittently, being separated by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*).
Second, there are the causes and conditions that enable those phenomena to manifest,
namely, consciousness that is stained by craving for the various sensual desires or for the existence of a personal identity (*satkāya*).
This is because one does not thoroughly understand such consciousness stained by craving.
Consequently, they are swept away and submerged by craving for the transitory collection (*satkāya*).
Due to this disposition, they are unable to enter into that nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, through eight aspects, one can thoroughly understand and eliminate all faults.
Furthermore, from this point downward,
the eight aspects are then set forth,
culminating in the statement: "It should be known that herein the eighth aspect— the dharma of detachment and the dharma of cessation— is excluded."
By means of the remaining seven aspects, one contemplates all the defects of the three times; by means of the aspect of abandonment, one contemplates the renunciation thereof.
It should be understood that herein, one is called a "knower who has attained penetration" by virtue of the former [aspects].
The wisdom regarding the non-self of the contaminated [dharmas] prior to the stage [of the path of cultivation] is called "the vision of pure excellence" by virtue of what follows;
this refers to the wisdom within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The tenth [section] explains the distinction between teachers and disciples who expound the well-spoken and the ill-spoken through five aspects.
The first is by way of their abiding.
That is to say, non-Buddhists dwell in bustle and clamor,
whereas the Buddha-dharma dwells in tranquility;
secondly, by way of governing the assembly.
This refers to how non-Buddhists, among their own disciples and followers,
hope that the assembly will collectively recognize them as their teacher;
this is because the number of such non-Buddhist disciples is limited.
This is called "having measure.
Although the Tathāgata is the unsurpassed Great Teacher for all the immeasurable devas, humans, and the world, and is honored as such by them,
he harbors no expectations.
Third, it may be known through the definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) of the treatises.
Fourth, by means of establishing and elucidating the path,
one first distinguishes its external characteristics, which consist of seven phrases.

Regarding the seventh point, because one does not know the words that ought to be spoken as they truly are according to how they are spoken, it is called "lack of knowledge regarding the measure" (*apramāṇa-jñāna*).
Because one does not know the words spoken in this context as they truly are, it is called "lack of knowledge regarding the cause" (*ahetu-jñāna*).
Next, [the text] generally reveals that within the Buddha's teaching there are five reasons based on practice.
Furthermore, although the various non-Buddhists have no differing assertions and so forth,
[the author] first grants them [a provisional position] and subsequently refutes it.
The eleventh [point] explains that suffering and pleasure are indeterminate;
this is precisely the section denoted by the character "equal" (等) in the verse.
In the prose, the initial chapter first establishes the thesis (*siddhānta*).
Thus, suffering and pleasure each have four characteristics based on three factors;
these shall now be explained in sequence.
First, regarding the place of birth:
that which is called "joy" refers to those who have arisen in the third dhyāna;
it is spoken of in terms of the place where pleasant sensation increases.
Regarding the statement that "that which is accompanied by pleasure may be of two kinds among humans," Master Jing says: Among humans,
although suffering and pleasure arise [alternately], it is still designated as being "accompanied by pleasant feeling."
The Master Da said:
"When one is born among humans, the body is 'accompanied' because it is pursued by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); thus it is called 'that which is accompanied.
It contains the seeds of both suffering and pleasure."
Therefore, it is said that there are two kinds of "possibility" (*saṃbhava*).
Regarding the statement "not yet permanently free from pleasure," this refers to those in the fourth dhyāna and above;
although pleasure does not manifest, the seed of pleasure still persists.
It is called "not yet permanently free.
Here, "suffering" refers to those among the hungry ghosts and animals;
this is based on the fact that certain realms of hungry ghosts and animals consist exclusively of places where suffering is experienced, and thus are termed the "essential nature of suffering."
Question: Previously, it was stated that "pleasure" herein refers to the state of ultimate bliss found in the third dhyāna;
now, regarding "suffering," why do you not specify that it resides in the *naraka* (hells)?
Regarding the statement that "sorrow and suffering are pervasive," meaning they exist among hungry ghosts and animals:
the explanation says that this is indeed so according to the principles of reality.
Now, based on the fact that among the hungry ghosts and animals there is a portion that experiences nothing but suffering,
they are called "hungry ghosts and animals.
As for those whose suffering is pervasive, they are said to be in the *naraka* (hells).
He asked again:
"In the previous section on the accomplishment of the faculties within the *Viniścaya*,
it was stated that the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is accomplished but not active within the hells."
Now, for what reason is it said that sorrow and suffering are pervasive?
The explanation states:
this is based on the extreme intensity of the suffering experienced in the hells.
The arising of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) therein is also termed suffering (*duḥkha*);
therefore, it is said that "only suffering manifests.
This is now stated according to the distinction between the arising of sorrow and suffering within the six consciousnesses.
Therefore, it is said that sorrow and suffering are pervasive.
Next, according to the analysis of feeling (*vedanā*), it is further stated: "That which is called pleasure (*sukha*)..."
Regarding the state in which neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation is present,
Master Jing says:
when the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā*) arises, it is not painful, and is therefore also called pleasant.
Master Tai said:
"The sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant is called 'pleasure' because it is quiescent."
That which is "accompanied by pleasure" refers to the state when a painful sensation is present;
although it is painful at that time, if one subsequently encounters favorable conditions, pleasure arises,
and thus it is called "accompanied by pleasure."
Regarding "pervaded by joy and pleasure," this refers to the state when pleasure is manifest before one.
As for "not being permanently separated from pleasure":
Because the seeds of pleasure accompany [the mind] in all states,
that which is contrary to this should be called "suffering. This is the distinction between [pleasure and] suffering.
In the state when neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation is present,
that which is accompanied by suffering [is present]; in the state when pleasure is present, [that which is accompanied by suffering is present].
"Pervasive by sorrow and suffering" refers to the state when painful feeling is manifest.
"Not permanently separated from" means...
Because it is accompanied by the causes of suffering in all states,
the following is explained in terms of the time periods (*adhvan*).
Furthermore, "pleasure" refers to both conduct conducive to pleasure and that which has already ceased.
Regarding those past formations conducive to pleasant experience and those accompanied by pleasure that were initially pleasant:
this refers to the presence of the causes for pleasure that will give rise to pleasure in a future life.
Regarding "pervasion by joy and pleasure":
this refers to that which accords with a state of pleasure in the present— namely,
present conduct conducive to pleasure and pleasant sensation.
"Those who will forever be separated from happiness in the future" refers to others throughout the three periods of time;
they have emerged from the phenomena that produce pleasant feeling because they possess the causes of happiness.
The name is not yet permanently separated.
